newsitem.title: UK: British gilts' case grows stronger by the day.
newsitem.headline: British gilts' case grows stronger by the day.

text.p: Economists for months have been arguing that British bonds (gilts) look more attractive than other European markets, and another set of market-friendly British data on Thursday gave them added conviction.
Gilts have been unable to narrow their yield premium to benchmark German Bunds significantly this year but with two weeks to go before a British election, analysts said their time is nigh.
"My suspicion is that (after the election) we'll see gilts enjoy a major bull run," said Roger Bootle, HSBC Group chief economist and member of a British Treasury forecasting panel.
"I've been one of those people arguing gilts look outstandingly good value," Bootle said.
Many others also say they have been on the gilt bandwagon.
"I've just spent 10 days in America telling people they're extremely attractive," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW in London. "I didn't find much disagreement."
Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident, was another gilt fan. "I'm of the camp that says gilts can be expected to outperform," he said.
So why have gilts failed to outperform?
Bootle said one reason was simply uncertainty in the market, about British post-election economic policy and what will happen externally about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Milligan, said people in the market want to know what kind of mix the next government will choose between fiscal and monetary policy, even with the current subdued price growth and forecasts for lower inflation.
"If you're looking at the long end of the curve they really are worried about whether inflation is going to be kept under control," Milligan said.
But on Thursday, the Office for National Statistics said British underlying inflation was 2.7 percent in the year to March. This is barely above the 2.5 percent government target.
Milligan and Bootle both argued that with sterling so strong and compettion among retailers, lower inflation in Britain could be expected.
But analysts are still waiting for a green light.
"The gilt market is good value -- the problem is what's going to trigger that value to be realised," said Adams of BZW.
Would it be the British election, a turn in the economic cycle in Europe, the single currency process?
"There's a whole range of potential triggers out there," Adams said.

The 7.25 percent gilt due 2007 currently trades at a yield spread of 181 basis points over the 6.0 percent Bund due 2007. The spread has been in a broad 140 to 200 basis point range for two years but has been edging higher since February.
For Adams, and other analysts, outperformance by gilts was a matter of when, not if.
"Fundamentally you can make a case for the spread narrowing to a range of 100 to 125 basis points. There's a lot of potential outperformance after the UK election," he said.

He said the whole EMU debate was a potential win-win equation for gilts. On the one hand, if it appeared that Spain and Italy would be out of EMU, gilts offered an attractive alternative to those high yielders. Gilt yields are currently just above those of Italian BTPs and well above Spanish Bonos.
"Looking at it the other way, if they (Italy and Spain) are in, do you want to own Bunds? No you don't. Either way you can view cash flowing into gilts," Adams said.
Bootle of HSBC added that sterling had been able to reap the benefits of EMU uncertainty but that gilts had not, suggesting there was scope for gilts still to gain from this factor.
He agreed that a 100-125 basis point spread was not unreasonable for gilts.
